title: Unresponsive / CPR
summary: Someone collapsed or won't wake up: check breathing, start CPR, use an AED.
sources: American Heart Association Guidelines for CPR and Emergency Cardiovascular Care
Wilderness Medical Society Clinical Practice Guidelines
firstLine: Make sure the scene is safe for you. Shout for help. If anyone can reach 911, have them call now and bring an AED if one exists.

nodes.prompt: Tap their shoulder hard and shout. Do they respond?

nodes.help: Look at the chest for 5 to 10 seconds. Occasional gasps are NOT normal breathing. If cold and possibly hypothermic, look for up to 1 minute.

nodes.title: Start CPR - adult
steps: Lay them on their back on a firm surface.
Put the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top.
Push hard and fast: at least 2 inches deep, 100 to 120 pushes per minute (the beat of "Stayin' Alive").
Let the chest come all the way back up between pushes.
If trained and willing: after every 30 pushes, tilt the head back, lift the chin, and give 2 breaths that make the chest rise. If not, do continuous pushes only.
For drowning, give breaths if you can. Oxygen is the main problem.
doNot: Do not stop pushes for more than 10 seconds.
Do not be afraid of hurting them. Broken ribs are common and survivable; no CPR is fatal.

nodes.title: Start CPR - child
steps: Lay them on their back on a firm surface.
Use one or two hands on the center of the chest.
Push about 2 inches deep (one third of the chest depth), 100 to 120 pushes per minute.
Let the chest come all the way back up between pushes.
If trained: give 2 breaths after every 30 pushes (15 if two rescuers). Breaths matter more for children.
doNot: Do not stop pushes for more than 10 seconds.

nodes.title: Start CPR - infant
steps: Lay the baby on their back on a firm surface.
Circle the chest with both hands and push with both thumbs (or use the heel of one hand), on the breastbone just below the nipple line.
Push about 1.5 inches deep (one third of the chest depth), 100 to 120 per minute.
Give 2 gentle breaths after every 30 pushes: cover the baby's mouth and nose with your mouth and puff just enough to make the chest rise.
doNot: Do not tilt the head far back. A neutral, sniffing position opens an infant's airway.

nodes.title: Use the AED
steps: Turn it on and follow its voice prompts.
Bare and dry the chest. Stick the pads where the pictures show.
Make sure nobody is touching the person when it analyzes or shocks.
Restart chest pushes right after each shock or "no shock advised."

nodes.title: Keep going
steps: Keep doing CPR. Switch rescuers every 2 minutes to stay strong.
Stop only if they start breathing normally or move, a trained responder takes over, the scene becomes unsafe, or you are physically unable to continue.

options.label: Long time, no signs of life, no help coming

nodes.title: Recovery position
steps: Roll them onto their side, top knee bent, head tilted back slightly so fluid can drain from the mouth.
If an injury to the neck or back is likely, keep them on their back and hold the head still unless they vomit.
Keep them warm.
Check their breathing every minute or two.

nodes.title: They are responsive
steps: Ask what happened and what hurts. Look for bleeding and injuries.
Keep them still and warm. Do not let them get up if they collapsed.
Chest pain, trouble breathing, one-sided weakness, slurred speech, or confusion means they need a hospital urgently.
If they become unresponsive, start this protocol again.

nodes.title: Unresponsive but breathing
steps: Keep them in the recovery position and warm.
Never leave them alone. Check breathing every minute or two.
Get them to medical care as soon as you can.
If breathing stops, start CPR immediately.

nodes.title: Handed off
steps: Tell the responder when they collapsed, when CPR started, and how many AED shocks were given.
Share the handoff log below.

nodes.title: Prolonged CPR without help
steps: Without advanced care, survival after about 30 minutes of CPR with no signs of life is extremely unlikely.
Exceptions: cold-water drowning, severe hypothermia, or lightning strike. Keep going longer if it is safe to do so.
Stopping is a judgment call when you are exhausted or your group is put at risk. You are not to blame. You gave them their only chance.
